perspective:
From Gloria Bangura’s perspective:

- I work as an administrative assistant at a large event planning company. Donald is a part-time bartender at company events. We’re colleagues, but not personally close; we mostly interact during events.
- At several events, I noticed Donald seemed distracted and lacked enthusiasm while serving drinks. I thought he might be unhappy with his job.
- I asked him if everything was okay with the job. He said he was “just not as into it as I used to be” and that it was “kind of repetitive.”
- After thinking about that conversation, I suspected his dissatisfaction might be connected to larger personal issues. I suggested he consider talking to a professional. He said he hadn’t considered it and wasn’t sure it would help.
- I then sensed a change in his behavior toward me and worried he might resent my suggestion or feel I overstepped. I told him I only wanted to help and didn’t mean to make assumptions about his life. He said he was “a bit taken aback at first” but knew I meant well, and that it was “a lot to process.”
- I felt we had cleared the air and wanted to strengthen our working relationship. I invited him to collaborate on a new project, saying it could use his creative input. He thanked me, said he appreciated it, wanted to be more involved, and called it a great opportunity.
- After we successfully collaborated, I observed his significant contributions and renewed enthusiasm. I believed he was a valuable team member and wanted him to feel appreciated. I publicly acknowledged his work in a team meeting. He thanked me, said it meant a lot to him, was glad he could contribute, and that it felt great to be appreciated.
